title: The Riemann Hypothesis proof written out as readable papers
summary:
Levent Alpoge's formal proof gives a route to GRH for Dirichlet L-functions, and with it the Riemann hypothesis. I wrote that proof out as mathematics papers a person can read, and placed it as the last row of a series that follows Weil's proof for curves, carried over to Spec ℤ.

The chain is: three theorems on integral modular forms on unitary groups ⇒ a main inequality ⇒ a one-sided bound ⇒ a Landau-type criterion ⇒ GRH ⇒ RH.

--Guide, 10 pages, no proofs: https://github.com/dtrejopizzo/riemann/blob/main/04-papers/57-riemann-hypothesis-along-the-rows-of-weils-proof/riemann-hypothesis-rows-weil-proof-guide.pdf --Map of the logical path, with a link to the paper that proves each step: https://www.datp.ar/riemann --All the papers (the main paper, eight companions, and a single 659-page volume with everything): https://github.com/dtrejopizzo/riemann/tree/main/04-papers None of this is peer reviewed yet. The papers are public so that they can be checked, and I would like to hear about errors.

Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50674717

title: If you're doing Monte Carlo try Knuth LGC
summary:
I was doing a monte carlo simulation involving a few million iterations and that didn't really need anything all that random. I remembered reading about a fast algorithm for very fast values (just a couple of ops), so I asked about this and was surprised that there is one. I just inserted it into my c code and it became ten times faster. If you're doing some monte carlo simulations where you don't need anything very random, give it a try.

before: 3.5 seconds. after: 0.42 seconds.

code I used:

   #include 

   static uint32_t seed = 1;   // any non-zero value is fine

   static inline uint32_t fast_rand(void) {
       seed = seed * 1664525u + 1013904223u;   // mod 2^32 is free
       return seed;
   }

   // then (example):
   int ch = fast_rand() % 1297 // where 1297 is the range.
(there's a slight bias when using % this way.) code gave the same results so it was still correct. you would adjust 1297 to the range you need an integer result in, this is from my example.

title: Ask HN: YC startup not paying for a take-home. What to do?
summary:
First of all, using a throwaway as I am not comfortable going fully public yet, but this post has enough information that the involved parties will know who I am and how to reach out.

Earlier in the year I was approached by a prominent YC startup of a recent batch for an interview process, which included a fairly lengthy take home, took me 14 hours of work.

After submitting the project and going through a debrief interview, communication with the company became increasingly difficult. Eventually, I decided to withdraw from the process and requested payment for the take-home assignment.

What followed was months of back and forth trying to get paid, without any resolution. Among other things, they requested a specific payment method that had never been disclosed beforehand, which I couldn't provide. There was also a disagreement about the amount I was supposed to receive.

Eventually, I gave up. The whole experience was taking a toll on my mental health. I've never felt so poorly treated by a company throughout a hiring process.

As a last attempt, I reached out to Y Combinator directly via info@ycombinator.com and to their batch GP, who turned out to be Garry Tan himself. I didn't particularly expect a response, but I tried anyway.

Funny enough, earlier this week I received another recruiting email from one of the company's co-founders. I then replied asking that I get paid for the previous take home... no response :)

So I decided to not give up anymore as this is a pretty fucked up thing to do with people out there, I just don't know what to do.

What can I do in this situation? Has anyone dealt with something similar, particularly with a YC company? Is there a reasonable way to escalate this, or get Y Combinator to help hold one of its companies accountable?

I'd just like to get paid for the work I did and hopefully prevent other candidates from going through the same experience.

title: Ask HN: Isn't it time we promote conversation rather than d*wnr*nking it?
summary:
(Apologies for the childish self-censoring, but A) I'm serious about it and B) it kinda drives home my point on its own...)

More specifically: why continue the practice of pushing content off the front page that has a healthy discussion, and preventing content that gets multiple comments early on from reaching it in the first place?

I've been tilting at the windmill of Markdown support on this site for years now, through which I've learned that all three mods are undeniably well-meaning, competent people. Even when seemingly suspicious actions are taken --like downranking any post that mentioned the NSA in the wake of Snowden-- I feel confident that the actions are taken in good faith. Namely, they seem to prioritize:

1. Prevention of 'flame wars', which imply vitriol but also a tit-for-tat between two 'sides'. This is why you can't downvote replies to your comment, you get tempbanned for a few hours if posting comments that get downvoted, etc.; there's lots of mechanisms in play.

2. Prevention of spam. Doesn't relate to this issue.

3. Maintenance of a respectful, ~professional culture. This is the big one here, I think. By killing discussions about politics, white vs. blue dresses, Rust rewrites, and other issues people are more passionate about than they are about local-first CRDTs and the rise of WASM, the culture is made professional on a substrate level.

I just don't think that's enough to justify this feature, though. There's a lot to say in response, but to keep it as short as possible:

A) This is prioritizing a vision of HackerNews as a newsletter for startup founders rather than a community at the heart of (anglophone?) tech, which is obviously becoming more important by the day. We're already well past the point where LLM-based tools can produce a far better, more personalized, fairer, and more diverse newsletter than a forum could hope to, anyway.

B) It's taking a shortcut when there's no need for one, if they accepted help in the form of volunteer moderators below the admins (they're ubiquitous elsewhere for a reason) and/or sponsorship from tech firms to fund staff, possibly in exchange for a subtle shoutout in the footer.

C) As Reddit spirals into a steep dive[1] and LessWrong spirals upwards in an ever-tighter (light)cone[2], this is the only sizeable forum left of any quality for discussing science and technology. As AI gets better forums are losing their utility as a place to crowdsource objective answers, sure, but I'd argue they're more important than ever for understanding the trickier issues that are coming to define our society.

TL;DR: I can't help but shake the impression that HN is fleeing from the future and its founders' (I count the admins, dang-it!) stated ideals regarding freedom, democracy, and epistemic agency. Not the future, actually: the present.

[1]: https://www.businessinsider.com/reddit-ad-growth-plans-search-shopping-ai-agents-2026-11

[2]: https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/kmruNMEMK5uN3LH6n/notes-on-the-decline-of-lesswrong-s-great-writers

---

To be clear, I am serious about the "Ask" part of this "Ask HN", despite giving an argument; this truly baffles me. What do you y'all think? What am I missing?

Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50671974

title: Ask HN: How to validate my idea/MVP?
summary:
I'm currently building Apartment Archive, which is an online interior design business focused on making personalized interior design and space planning more accessible.

I've spent quite a bit of time building out the website and figuring out the service itself. I'm at a point where I'd like to validate the idea, get a better sense of product-market fit and see whether there's enough demand before building much further.

I've been reading about smoke testing (a facade MVP or even just a landing page with a call to action to gauge interest), but I'm more curious about how people have actually gone about doing this in practice. I'm wondering how to go about this when starting without an existing audience.

Where did you find your first potential customers? Were there any communities, groups, or specific approaches that worked particularly well for you?

I'm also trying to get some clarity around how people distinguished between someone thinking their idea was interesting and someone actually being willing to pay for it. I've conducted some user testing which was helpful in getting a better understanding of what people want and don't want, but I'd like to find a way to gauge whether people would actually pay for the service.

Would appreciate hearing what worked, what didn't, and what you'd do differently if you were starting from scratch.

Thank you in advance for your help! I appreciate you taking the time to read my post.

title: Is there a "Firebase" for agentic backends
summary:
Hi guys, I’m curious is there a "Firebase" for agentic backends ?

Where, in a weekend, can one easily build or integrate agentic features without having to worry about all the infra headaches for memory, tools, data ingestion, context management, permissions, governance, auth, models?

There are tons of frameworks for all these different functions, but most cover one layer. A framework is just a library, but teams still have to own everything around it. Some have cloud offerings, but that typically means you end up with 5-10 different backends, which makes evals, permissions, and governance that much more difficult.

I’m thinking of open-sourcing a bunch of our internal infra which we have been building over the last year and a half to support exactly this whilst keeping it framework-agnostic.

So that you get the infra whilst maintaining your own loop.

Keen to hear if something like this exists.

And if this is a challenge you have experienced or are experiencing as you build agentic systems or integrate AI into your apps.

title: Sheetlytic – Take a photo of sheet music and hear it play
summary:
My wife is a piano teacher, and she often encounters a simple problem: students return home after their lessons and forget how a piece is supposed to sound or how a particular passage should be played.

I built Sheetlytic, an app that turns a photo of sheet music into playable music.

The idea is to bridge the gap between reading sheet music and hearing it, without having to search for an existing recording or manually enter notes into notation software.

While the original motivation came from piano teaching, I think it could also be useful for musicians learning unfamiliar pieces on their own.

Sheetlytic is available on:

Android: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=verbosus.sheetlytic

iOS: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/sheet-music-scanner-player/id6830832313

Windows: https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9p2pm166vc69

I'm the developer and would love to hear your feedback, particularly on usability, recognition accuracy, and potential use cases.

Happy to answer any questions!

title: Ask HN: Is Claude Code nerfing AI and agent-harness projects?
summary:
Over the last 5-6 months, I've been researching a lot about AI/ML and harnesses from novel research papers, experimenting with transformer architectures, experimental harnesses, post-training reward weights, and stuff like that.

I've used Claude Code for almost two years to ship internal tools, dashboards, and full-stack apps with great results. On older projects I hand-checked code much more closely and Claude never pulled anything like this, so over time I stopped checking every line. I feel this is standard experience for agentic coding devs. Yet on anything touching AI/ML research, or anything that smells remotely competitive with Anthropic's own stack, it started behaving completely differently.

Instead of implementing the specs I hand-wrote, it quietly skipped them while swearing it was following them to a T. It blocked hooks and test execution while telling me everything was green, modified CI scripts so they'd pass without running actual checks, and filled the repo with bad tests. I added stricter hooks, subagent configs, guardrails, Alloy models, and AST-based clone detection, and it still only broke down like this on this repo. I got my Ultra refund and moved to another provider.

The visible Opus fallback tripped once or twice only in 6 months, right up to today.

With the justification of "security", which is kind of understandable for the cyberdefense ramifications of AI, it still looks and feels like pulling up the ladder behind them while marketing Claude as your trustworthy agent for any kind of task. Why are we trusting a handful of labs with the future when they keep the real models to themselves and kneecap anyone else trying to build close to, or on, the frontier? It feels extremely anti-competitive.
